slides.title: Chapter 4: Keys and Addresses

items.cap: Figure 4-2, Mastering Bitcoin 3rd edition, CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.notes: Chapter 3 showed the software that checks the rules. Chapter 4 opens the smallest secret it protects, a private key, and follows it to the address that people read aloud. Every number in this deck was computed with the chapter's own Python library.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.take: Five parts, three true stories, twenty-one examples
slides.notes: The route has five parts that follow one secret from a number to an address. Three true stories and twenty-one code examples are spread across them, and every example has a picture of its result.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers

items: What is a private key, and what makes one safe to use?
How does a private key become a public key, and why can it not be reversed?
How does a public key become a legacy address, and why does it carry a checksum?
What do P2SH, Bech32 and Bech32m change about addresses?
How is a private key written down so that a wallet can import it?
Why can an address be valid and still have no key behind it?

slides.notes: The six questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all six has understood the chapter.

slides.title: The chapter in one picture
slides.take: Random bits, a key, a point, a hash, an address
slides.notes: One secret travels five steps. Random bits become a private key, the curve turns it into a public key, two hashes shorten it, and an encoding with a checksum makes the address. The parts of this deck follow the same path.

slides.title: Public Key Cryptography
slides.sub: From one secret number to a point that nobody can run backwards

items.meaning: A secret 256-bit number; whoever knows it can spend the coins.
items.analogy: Think of the one key to your front door.

items.meaning: A point on the curve computed from the private key; safe to publish.
items.analogy: Think of the lock on your door: everyone can see it.

items.meaning: The curve y squared equals x cubed plus 7 that Bitcoin uses.
items.analogy: Think of the one game board that every player agrees on.

slides.notes: Part 1 starts with the secret itself. A private key is only a number, a public key is a point computed from it, and the curve makes that computation a one-way street.

slides.title: The 1976 paper that split the key in two
slides.sub: 3 June 1976 · public-key cryptography is born

items.cap: Picture: Whitfield Diffie, 2017 - Duncan Hull, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHO Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, cryptographers at Stanford; both received the 2015 Turing Award.
WHAT The paper 'New Directions in Cryptography': a key split into a public half and a private half.
WHEN 1976-06-03 (manuscript received; printed in November 1976)
WHERE Stanford University, California; IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, volume IT-22.
WHY Secret keys had to be carried to every partner; the authors wanted to remove that need.
HOW Each user publishes one half and keeps the other; a one-way computation links them, as in this chapter.

items.who: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, the Stanford researchers who wrote the paper and received the Turing Award for it
items.where: IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, volume IT-22, number 6

slides.take: Every address in this chapter stands on one 1976 idea
slides.notes: In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman asked whether two people could talk privately without first sharing a secret. Their answer was a key split in two. Bitcoin's elliptic-curve multiplication is a later form of the same idea.

slides.title: A private key is a number below n
slides.sub: The book's example key, and the edges of the range
slides.take: Any whole number from 1 to n minus 1 is a key
slides.notes: A private key is a very large number between 1 and n minus 1. Zero and n itself are not allowed. Every number inside the range is a valid key, which is why choosing one at random is safe.

slides.title: Entropy: bits an attacker must guess
slides.sub: Why a Bitcoin key needs 256 fair coin flips
slides.take: Only truly random choices reach the 256 bits of a key
slides.notes: Entropy counts how many bits of guessing a secret withstands. A PIN has 13 bits and a long password 79. Only 256 fair coin flips match a Bitcoin key, so a key must come from a proper random source.

slides.title: The curve secp256k1 and its generator
slides.sub: Checking that G really lies on the curve
slides.take: The curve is one short formula: y squared = x cubed + 7
slides.notes: Bitcoin's curve is y squared equals x cubed plus 7, counted modulo a 256-bit prime. We test that the generator point G satisfies the formula. Every public key starts from this one fixed point.

slides.title: Points on a curve: doubling G
slides.take: Tangent, meeting point, mirror image: that is one doubling
slides.notes: Figure 4-4 shows one doubling on the curve of figure 4-2. Draw the tangent at G, find where it meets the curve again, and mirror that point across the x-axis. The result is 2G, and repeating the step gives 4G and 8G.

slides.title: Doubling and adding: k times G
slides.sub: How one multiplication reaches a huge number
slides.take: Doubling reaches a 256-bit key in a few hundred steps
slides.notes: Multiplying G by k means adding G to itself k times. Doubling makes this fast: a key of 253 bits needs a few hundred doublings and additions, not 10 to the 76 steps.

slides.title: The point at infinity on a toy curve
slides.sub: A curve over 17 numbers, small enough to list
slides.take: Multiples of a point repeat; the cycle closes at infinity
slides.notes: On a toy curve we can list every multiple of a point. The ninth multiple is the point at infinity, the zero of the curve, and then the list starts over. Bitcoin's curve works the same way with a vastly larger cycle.

slides.title: One-way: the work to find a key
slides.sub: Why the public key cannot be run backwards
slides.take: Each extra bit doubles the attacker's work
slides.notes: Finding k from k times G means trying keys one by one, about half of them on average. A 20-bit key falls after half a million tries. A 256-bit key needs about 10 to the 77, which is out of reach.

slides.title: Legacy Addresses
slides.sub: From a public key to the address that people read aloud

items.meaning: Pay to public key hash: the output script holds only a 20-byte hash.
items.analogy: Think of a locker that shows a number, never the shape of the key.

items.meaning: SHA256 followed by RIPEMD-160: the 20-byte hash of a public key.
items.analogy: Think of two sieves in a row: the finer one decides.

items.meaning: Version byte, payload and checksum written in base58.
items.analogy: Think of a parcel with a label, a content and a seal.

slides.notes: Part 2 turns a public key into the first kind of Bitcoin address. Two hashes shorten the key to twenty bytes, and Base58Check adds a version and a checksum that catches typing mistakes.

slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: These rows pair each concept of the part Legacy Addresses with something you already know. Say the meaning first, then the comparison, in your own words. The code slides that follow run the same ideas.

slides.title: A public key has two encodings
slides.sub: Compressed keys keep x and the parity of y
slides.take: A compressed key is 33 bytes; the full one is 65
slides.notes: A public key is a point with two coordinates. The uncompressed form writes both after a 04 byte. The compressed form writes x and one byte for the parity of y, and y is recovered from x.

slides.title: P2PK holds the key, P2PKH only its hash
slides.sub: Two output scripts for the same public key
slides.take: P2PKH shows a commitment to the key, not the key
slides.notes: The original output script, P2PK, contains the public key itself. P2PKH contains only a 20-byte hash of it. The hash is a commitment: the key is revealed only when the coins are spent.

slides.title: HASH160 is SHA256 then RIPEMD-160
slides.sub: Two hashes turn a 33-byte key into 20 bytes
slides.take: Two hashes in a row: 33 bytes in, 20 bytes out
slides.notes: HASH160 first applies SHA256 and then RIPEMD-160. The 33-byte key becomes 32 bytes and then 20 bytes. The result is the number that a legacy address stands for.

slides.title: Why 58? Satoshi left the reasons in the file
slides.sub: 8 January 2009 · a design memo inside base58.h

items.cap: Picture: Satoshi bust, Budapest - Fekist, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons - a stand-in, since the author's face is unknown

items: WHO Satoshi Nakamoto, the pseudonymous author of Bitcoin's first software; the file's copyright line names him.
WHAT A comment in base58.h that lists four reasons for dropping 0, O, I and l and all punctuation.
WHEN 2009-01-08 (version 0.1 announced; the memo's own date is not recorded)
WHERE The file src/base58.h in the bitcoin/bitcoin source tree on GitHub.
WHY People copy addresses by hand, in e-mail and by double-click, so the text must survive all three.
HOW Of 62 letters and digits the four look-alikes go, so 58 remain: the alphabet of every legacy address.

items.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, named by the file's own copyright line
items.where: src/base58.h in the bitcoin/bitcoin source tree

slides.take: Address formats are human-factors engineering, written into the source
slides.notes: The first lines of base58.h are a design memo. It gives four human reasons: look-alike characters, punctuation that breaks selection, line breaks in e-mail, and double-clicking. The alphabet of every legacy address is a usability decision.

slides.title: Base58Check, step by step
slides.sub: Version, hash and checksum become an address
slides.take: An address is 25 bytes written in 34 characters
slides.notes: A legacy address has three parts: a version byte, the 20-byte key hash and a four-byte checksum. Written in base58 they give a 34-character string. The leading 00 version byte becomes the first character, 1.

slides.title: From public key to address
slides.take: Each arrow is a function that you have just run
slides.notes: Figure 4-7 is the whole road from public key to address. SHA256 and RIPEMD-160 shrink the key to 20 bytes, a version byte and a checksum make 25, and base58 writes them as 34 characters. Each step is a function you have just run.

slides.title: The checksum catches every single typo
slides.sub: Every one-character mistake, tried one by one
slides.take: A single typo is caught almost every time
slides.notes: We change one character of the address in every possible way: 1,938 variants. A wallet that checks the four-byte checksum rejects every one of them. A random typo passes only about once in 4.3 billion.

slides.title: Script Hashes and Bech32
slides.sub: Addresses that commit to a script, and the second alphabet

items.meaning: Pay to script hash: spending reveals the script and then satisfies it.
items.analogy: Think of a locked briefcase opened in front of the cashier.

items.meaning: SegWit addresses in lowercase letters and digits with a stronger checksum.
items.analogy: Think of a postcode that also detects a mistyped letter.

items.meaning: The same encoding with a new checksum constant, used from witness version 1.
items.analogy: Think of a corrected second edition of the same form.

slides.notes: Part 3 covers the addresses that came after the first kind. P2SH commits to a whole script, and SegWit's Bech32 and Bech32m add a version, a program and a stronger checksum.

slides.title: Bech32: concepts (1 of 2)
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: These rows pair each concept of the part Script Hashes and Bech32 with something you already know. Say the meaning first, then the comparison, in your own words. The code slides that follow run the same ideas.

slides.title: Bech32: concepts (2 of 2)
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: These rows pair each concept of the part Script Hashes and Bech32 with something you already know. Say the meaning first, then the comparison, in your own words. The code slides that follow run the same ideas.

slides.title: P2SH commits to a whole script
slides.sub: A two-of-three multisignature behind one address
slides.take: A P2SH address hides the script until spending
slides.notes: P2SH lets an address stand for any script. We build a two-of-three multisignature script of 105 bytes and hash it with HASH160. The address starts with 3 and reveals the script only when the coins are spent.

slides.title: Collision and preimage: bits of work
slides.sub: Why a 160-bit hash is weaker for scripts
slides.take: A collision costs only half the bits of a hash
slides.notes: Finding any two inputs with one hash takes about 2 to the n over 2 tries; finding an input for a given hash takes 2 to the n. A 160-bit hash gives only 80 bits against collisions, which is why SegWit scripts use SHA256.

slides.title: A Bech32 address, taken apart
slides.sub: Network, version, program and checksum
slides.take: Split at the last 1: name, version, program, checksum
slides.notes: A Bech32 address has four parts. The network name bc, a separator 1, the data and a six-letter checksum. The first data letter is the witness version, and the rest is the witness program.

slides.title: Witness version and witness program
slides.sub: Three addresses from the book, decoded
slides.take: Version 0 for older SegWit; version 1 for Taproot
slides.notes: The decoder returns the witness version and the program. Version 0 holds a 20-byte key hash or a 32-byte script hash. Version 1 holds a 32-byte Taproot key and makes the address start with bc1p.

slides.title: Bech32 accepts the extra q, Bech32m does not
slides.sub: The weakness that Bech32m repaired
slides.take: Bech32m changed one constant and closed the gap
slides.notes: In Bech32 a q inserted before a final p leaves the checksum valid, so a typo can go unnoticed. The strings from the book all pass the old check and fail the new one. Bech32m changes the constant to close the gap.

slides.title: Private Key Formats
slides.sub: The same private key, written in the forms a wallet can import

items.meaning: Wallet import format: Base58Check of a version byte 80 and the key.
items.analogy: Think of a key packed in a labelled travel case.

items.meaning: WIF with a final 01 byte that marks the key as compressed.
items.analogy: Think of a luggage tag that says travel light.

items.meaning: Not a smaller key: a flag that tells a wallet to use compressed public keys.
items.analogy: Think of a note that says use the short form of my name.

slides.notes: Part 4 is about writing a private key down. The same number can appear as hex or as WIF, and one extra byte tells the wallet whether to use compressed public keys.

slides.title: Formats: concepts
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: These rows pair each concept of the part Private Key Formats with something you already know. Say the meaning first, then the comparison, in your own words. The code slides that follow run the same ideas.

slides.title: WIF: a private key dressed for travel
slides.sub: Base58Check of version 80, the key and a flag
slides.take: The final 01 byte says: use compressed public keys
slides.notes: Wallet import format wraps the private key in Base58Check. The version byte is 80. A trailing 01 byte, added only for compressed keys, makes the string one byte longer and changes its first letter to K or L.

slides.title: One private key, two addresses
slides.sub: Compressed and uncompressed keys hash differently
slides.take: The flag in WIF decides which address a wallet watches
slides.notes: One private key gives two public key encodings, and each hashes to a different address. Coins sent to one address are not seen at the other. The compressed flag in the WIF tells a wallet which one to use.

slides.title: Advanced Keys and Addresses
slides.sub: Chosen prefixes, printed keys and an address with no key

items.meaning: A vanity address starts with chosen letters, found by trying many keys.
items.analogy: Think of a custom number plate you must keep applying for.

items.meaning: A key and its address printed on paper and kept offline.
items.analogy: Think of a banknote locked in a drawer.

items.meaning: A hash that fixes a value now and lets you reveal it later.
items.analogy: Think of a sealed envelope holding your prediction.

slides.notes: Part 5 goes beyond a plain random key. A vanity address costs work in proportion to its letters, a paper wallet must be tested, and a valid address can still have no key.

slides.title: Advanced: concepts
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: These rows pair each concept of the part Advanced Keys and Addresses with something you already know. Say the meaning first, then the comparison, in your own words. The code slides that follow run the same ideas.

slides.title: Vanity search: 58 times harder per letter
slides.sub: Trying keys until the address starts as chosen
slides.take: Every extra letter costs about 58 times more work
slides.notes: A vanity address is found by trying keys until the text fits. One chosen letter is quick. Each further letter divides the chance by 58, so six letters need about 38 billion tries, and the work cannot be shortcut.

slides.title: A paper wallet must give back its address
slides.sub: Print, scan and check before funding
slides.take: Test the paper before you put coins on it
slides.notes: A paper wallet prints a WIF key and its address. Before any coins are sent, decode the WIF and confirm that the key reproduces the printed address. A smudged character is found while the paper is still empty.

slides.title: The address that eats coins
slides.sub: 6 October 2026 · figures fetched from a block explorer

items.cap: Picture: Bitcoin logo - Grayliptrot, public domain, Wikimedia Commons - a stand-in, since an address has no picture

items: WHO Thousands of anonymous senders; Blockstream Explorer recorded their deposits. Nobody holds the key.
WHAT The valid address 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE holds 13.41747849 bitcoin in 5,832 outputs, none ever spent.
WHEN 2026-10-06 (the day this balance was fetched)
WHERE The Bitcoin main chain; the address page of blockstream.info shows every deposit.
WHY A checksum catches typing mistakes, not a missing key, so wallets accept the address and the coins stay.
HOW A message was written in base58 letters, and the last letters were chosen so that the checksum fits.

items.who: Blockstream Explorer, whose address page and API recorded the deposits of thousands of anonymous senders
items.where: the Bitcoin main chain, at address 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE

slides.take: An address commits to a key; it does not prove that a key exists
slides.notes: This address was made by spelling a message and then closing it with letters that satisfy the checksum. No private key exists for it. Thousands of senders still paid into it, and not one coin has ever left.

slides.title: The eater address is valid but keyless
slides.sub: A message spelled in base58, with a good checksum
slides.take: A valid checksum is not proof that a key exists
slides.notes: The address spells a message in base58 letters and then closes with letters that make the checksum right. Wallets accept it without a warning. Nobody holds a key for it, so coins sent there are gone for good.

slides.title: Summary: the six answers
slides.take: Entropy, a point, a hash, a checksum, a flag, no key
slides.notes: Each row answers one of the six opening questions in a line. If you can say each answer in your own words, using the everyday pictures of this chapter, you have the chapter.
